endorsements.quote: Safe-harbor protection should therefore apply only to tools that hold Ministry of Food and Drug Safety marketing approval, maintain a Ministry of Food and Drug Safety–recognized quality management system, and operate under a PCCP analogous to the US Food and Drug Administration’s final guidance [ 11 ].

First, AI outputs must function as decision-support inputs rather than autonomous directives, with final clinical authority retained by a licensed physician or, where permitted under the proposed MSA amendment, a supervised EMT.
Third, adverse outcomes linked to AI-assisted decisions should trigger institutional postevent review by a designated clinical safety officer, with reporting to the relevant authority.
To support fair, safe, and trusted nationwide implementation, equity monitoring metrics, AI quality thresholds, and competency training for physicians and EMTs should be embedded in the system.
Equity indicators would provide ongoing surveillance for algorithmic bias across regions and facility types.

unlisted_practices: Amend the Medical Service Act to permit AI-supported telemedicine between emergency medical technicians and physicians during emergencies, limited to time-critical situations.
Mandate real-time, machine-readable disclosure of emergency department, ICU, and operating room capacity by designated emergency medical centers.
Add an emergency-use legal basis in the Personal Information Protection Act for real-time processing of sensitive data, with logging, role-based access, limited retention, and postevent notification.
Establish certification-linked safe-harbor protections for clinicians who use certified medical AI according to approved protocols with auditable logs and incident reporting.
Record all AI outputs and corresponding clinician decisions in immutable, timestamped audit logs accessible for regulatory review.
Use regulatory sandboxes with mandatory monitoring, incident reporting, and data collection to phase in AI-assisted teleconsultation and real-time biometric streaming.

Incorporate safeguards in matching algorithms, such as baseline inclusion policies, benchmarking by facility type, and capacity-adjustment buffers, to prevent AI routing from favoring well-resourced hospitals.
Use predetermined change control plans to support iterative AI model updates in emergency workflows.
Consult stakeholders including policymakers, emergency departments, EMTs, patient advocates, and AI developers when developing AI-EMS regulation.
